Updated read-through incorporating SLOOS:

- Policy stance: The FOMC kept the target range at 5.25–5.50% and continued balance-sheet runoff ($60B Treasuries, $35B agency MBS), stressing cumulative tightening and policy lags. Administered rates (IORB 5.4%, ON RRP 5.3%) and standing facilities keep tight control over short rates—clearly restrictive and anti-inflationary.

- SLOOS confirmation of tighter credit: The latest SLOOS indicates broad-based tightening in lending standards and terms. Banks reported tighter standards across:
  • Commercial real estate (CRE), including construction/land development and nonfarm nonresidential, with notable caution toward concentrated CRE exposures. 
  • Residential real estate (RRE), including GSE-eligible, government, QM non-jumbo, and jumbo segments, plus HELOCs.
  • Consumer credit, with tighter standards and terms for credit cards and auto loans.
  • C&I lending (including to both IG and below-IG firms, syndicated and non-syndicated), with weaker loan demand in several categories (e.g., subprime mortgages).
These results align with banks’ higher funding costs, liquidity and interest-rate risk management, and lower risk tolerance—especially pronounced among smaller/regional banks.

- Implications: SLOOS corroborates the FOMC’s warning that tighter credit conditions will weigh on activity and hiring and assist disinflation. With residual banking-sector vulnerabilities (CRE concentration, unrealized losses, deposit competition) and persistent policy restraint, the balance of risks to near-term growth leans softer even as long-run inflation credibility is supported.

Net tone shift: Given SLOOS’ broad tightening and pockets of weaker demand, the overall assessment moves from slightly positive to mildly negative for near-term growth/risk assets while still constructive for disinflation.
